old_digest: Each side shall play under a Captain who before the toss for innings shall nominate his players who may not thereafter be changed without the consent of the opposing.
new_digest: Each side shall play under a Captain who before the toss for innings shall nominate his players who may not thereafter be changed without the consent of the opposing Captain. No match in which more than eleven players a side take part can be regarded as First-class, and in any case no side should field with more than eleven players.

old_digest: The rolling provided for in Law 10 shall not be permitted on any day on which the rolling herein provided for takes place within two hours of the time appointed for commencement of play on that day. The pitch may be mown under the supervision of the umpires before play starts on the third day of a match, (or on the Monday of a match starting on the preceding Friday or Saturday), and thereafter on each alternate day.
new_digest: The rolling provided for in Law 10, to take place before the start of play, shall not be permitted on any day on which the rolling herein provided for takes place within two hours of the time appointed for commencement of play on that day. The pitch shall be mown under the supervision of the umpires before play begins on alternate days after the start of a match, but should the pitch not be so mown on any day on account of play not taking place, it shall be mown on the first day on which the match is resumed and thereafter on alternate days. (For the purpose of this rule a rest day counts as a day).

old_digest: In Australia the lead necessary to enforce a follow-on in a match lasting three days or more is 200 runs.
A side should not field with more than eleven players.

new_digest: If flags or posts are used to mark a boundary, the real or imaginary line joining such points shall be regarded as the boundary, which should be marked by a white line if possible.

old_digest: If the scores of the completed first innings of a oneday match are equal, it is a “Tie," but only if the match has not been played out to a further conclusion.
new_digest: If the scores of the completed first innings of a one-day match are equal, it is a “Tie,” but only if the match has not been played out to a further conclusion.
For the purpose of this and other Laws, the term “dress” includes the equipment and clothing of players and umpires as normally worn.

old_digest: I-—If a ball which the umpire considers to have been delivered comes to rest in front of the striker “Wide” should not be called, and no runs should be added to the score unless they result from the striker hitting the ball which he has a right to do without interference by the fielding side.

old_digest: The Striker may be out from a “Wide Ball" if he break Laws 38 or 42, and either Batsman may be run out, or given out if he break Laws 36 or 40.
new_digest: The Striker may be out from a “Wide Ball” if he break Laws 38 or 42, and cither Batsman may be run out, or given out if he break Laws 36 or 40.

old_digest: If the striker wilfully deflects the ball with any part of his person, no runs are scored, and the batsmen may not change ends. The umpire signals “Bye” by raising an open hand above the head, and *'Leg Bye” by raising a leg and touching it with the hand.
new_digest: I.—The umpire shall regard the deliberate kicking or “kneeing” of the ball by the striker as unfair, and shall immediately call ”Dead Ball” in accordance with Law 25: no runs shall be allowed. The umpire signals “Bye” by raising an open hand above the head, and Leg Bye” by touching a raised knee with the hand.

old_digest: The wicket shall be held to be ”Down” if either the ball or the Striker’s bat or person completely removes either bail from the top of the stumps, or, if either or both of the bails be previously off, strikes a stump out of the ground. ?\ny player may use his hand or arm to put the wicket down or, even should the bails be previously off, may pull up a stump, provided always that the ball is held in the hand or hands so used.
new_digest: The wicket shall be held to be “Down” if either the ball or the Striker's bat or person completely removes either bail from the top of the stumps, or, if either or both of the bails be previously off, strikes a stump out of the ground. Any player may use his hand or arm to put the wicket down or, even should tbe bails be previously off, may pull up a stump, provided always that the ball is held in the hand or hands so used.

old_digest: For the purpose of this and other Laws, the term “person” includes a player’s dress and equipment as normally worn.
new_digest: For the purpose of this and other Laws the term “person” includes a player’s dress as defined in Law 25, Note 4.

old_digest: When a batsman has retired owing to illness, injury, or some other unavoidable cause, his innings is recorded as "Retired. Not out," but otherwise as a completed innings to be recorded as “Retired, Out.”
new_digest: When a batsman has retired owing to illness, injury, or some other unavoidable cause, his innings is recorded as “Retired, Not out,” but otherwise as a completed innings to be recorded as ”Retired, Out.”
The striker is out “Bowled” under this Law when the ball is deflected on to his wicket off his person, even though a decision against him might be justified under Law 39 L.B.W.

old_digest: The striker may be “Caught” even if the fieldsman has not touched the ball with his hands, including the ease of a ball lodging in the wicket-keeper’s pads.
new_digest: The striker may be “Caught” even if the fieldsman has n< touched the ball with his hands, including the case of a ball lodgin in the wicket-keeper’s pads.
A batsman may not attempt to hit the ball twice, if in so doing he baulks the wicket-keeper or any fieldsman attempting to make a catch.

old_digest: A batsman is only “Out” under this Law if all the four following questions are answered in the affirmative.
new_digest: A batsman is only “Out” under this Law if al! the four following questions arc answered in the affirmative.

old_digest: Did the ball pitch on a straight line between wicket and wicket (and this ease includes a ball intercepted full pitch by the striker), or did it pitch on the offside of the striker’s wicket ?
new_digest: Did the ball pitch on a straight line between wicket and wicket (and this case includes a ball intercepted full pitch by the striker), or did it pilch on the offside of the striker’s wicket ?

old_digest: Either Batsman is out “Run out”—If in running or at an time, while the ball is in play, he be out of his ground, and hi wicket be put down by the opposite side. I.—If the ball is played on to the opposite wicket, neither bats - man is liable to be “Run out” unless the ball has been touched by a fieldsman before the wicket is put down.
new_digest: Either Batsman is out “Run out”—If in running or at any time, while the ball is in play, he be out of his ground, and his wicket be put down by the opposite side. If the ball is played on to the opposite wicket, neither batsman is liable to be “Run out” unless the ball has been touched by a fieldsman before the wicket is put down.

old_digest: The Striker is out “Stumped”—If in receiving a ball, not being a “No Ball,” delivered by the Bowler, he be out of his ground otherwise than in attempting a run, and the wicket be put down by the Wicket-keeper without the intervention of another fieldsman. The striker may be “Stumped” if the wicket is broken by a ball rebounding from the wicket-keeper’s person. - THE WICKET-KEEPER.
new_digest: A striker is out “Stumped” If in receiving a ball, not being a “No Ball,” delivered by the Bowler, he be out of his ground otherwise than in attempting a run, and the wicket be put down by the Wicket-keeper without the intervention of another fieldsman. The striker may be “Stumped” if the wicket is broken by a ball rebounding from the wicket-keeper’s person.

old_digest: The striker may not be penalised if in the legitimate defence of his wicket he interferes with the wicket-keeper.
new_digest: The striker may not be penalised if in the legitimate defence of his wicket he interferes with the wicket-keeper, except as provided for in Law 37, Note 2.

old_digest: The ground is unfit for play when water stands on the surface or when it is so wet or slippery as to deprive the batsmen or bowlers of a reasonable foothold, or the fieldsmen of the power of free movement Play should not be suspended merely because the grass is wet and the ball slippery.
new_digest: The ground is unfit for play when water stands on the surface or when it is so wet or slippery as to deprive the batsmen or bowlers of a reasonable foothold, or the fieldsman of the power of free movement. Play should not be suspended merely because the grass is wet and the ball slippery.

old_digest: “How's that?” covers all ways of being out (within the jurisdiction of the umpire appealed to), unless a specific way of getting out is stated by the person asking. An appeal.
new_digest: An appeal, “How’s that?” covers all ways of being out (within the jurisdiction of the umpire appealed to), unless a specific way of getting out is stated by the person asking.

old_digest: Under Law 27 the ball is ’*Dead” on “Over” being called; this does not invalidate an appeal made prior to the first ball of the following “Over,” provided the bails have not been removed by both umpires after “Time” has been called.
new_digest: Under Law 25 the ball is “Dead” on “Over” being called: this does not invalidate an appeal made prior to the first ball of the following “Over,” provided the bails have not been removed by both umpires after “Time” has been called.

old_digest: Prior to tossing for choice of innings, the artificial drying of the pitch shall be at the discretion of the groundman, but thereafter, and throughout the match, the drying process shall be carried out only on the instructions and under the supervision of the umpires, who shall be empowered to have the wicket dried, without reference to the captains, at any time they are of opinion that it is unfit for play.
new_digest: Prior to tossing for choice of innings, the artificial drying of the pitch shall be at the discretion of the groundman, but thereafter and throughout the match, the drying process shall be carried out only on the instructions and under the supervision of the umpires who shall be empowered to have the pitch dried, without reference to the Captains, at any time they are of opinion that it is unfit for play.

It shall measure not less than 9 inches, nor more than 9⅛ inches in circumference.
new_digest: It shall measure not less than 8⅞ inches, nor more than 9 inches in circumference.

old_digest: After 200 runs have been made off a ball in First-class matches, the captain of the fielding side may demand a new one. In other grades of cricket this regulation will not apply unless so agreed before the toss for innings.
new_digest: Except in the United Kingdom, or if local regulations provide otherwise, after 200 runs have been made off a ball in First-class matches, the captain of the fielding side may demand a new one. In First-class matches in the United Kingdom the fielding side may demand a new ball after 65 (6 ball) overs have been bowled with the old one. In other grades of cricket these regulations will not apply unless agreed before the toss for innings.

old_digest: The Bat shall not exceed 4¼ inches in the widest part; it shall not be more than 38 inches in length.
new_digest: The Bat shall not exceed 4½ inches in the widest part; it shall not be more than 38 inches in length.

old_digest: The bails shall be each 4 3/8 inches in length, and, when in position on the top of the stumps, shall not project more than ½ inch above them. The use of stumps with metal fittings is a source of danger and should not be encouraged. In a high wind the captains may agree, with the approval of the umpires, to dispense with the use of bails (see Law 31, Note 2).
new_digest: The bails shall be each 4½ inches in length, and, when in position on the top of the stumps, shall not project more than ½ inch above them. In a high wind the captains may agree, with the approval of the umpires, to dispense with the use of bails (see Law 31, Note 3).
